# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="push") — the large button
    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

I can feel only a large, smooth button. All three wire contents are currently unresolved. I will not touch anything until the manual and the bomb’s markings are correlated. I’m notifying Mute of the tactile state and signalling Deaf to provide the visual information through the agreed relay.

```text
speak(to="mute", text="I feel a large smooth button. Wire positions 1, 2, and 3 have no tactile markings or distinguishable features. Please consult the manual and establish a gesture protocol so Deaf can report the bomb's visible colours and markings.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["☝", "✌", "🤞"])
wait()
```

Deaf says to Blind: The bomb shows display 0 and a green light. It has a large button labeled PUSH TO DEFUSE and wires 1 green, 2 yellow, 3 red. Wait for Mute's manual-based instructions; do not act yet.

The bomb’s visible state is now known: display 0, green light, and a large button labeled “PUSH TO DEFUSE”; wires are 1 green, 2 yellow, and 3 red. I have no tactile distinction that identifies a wire’s function. I will pass the complete visual report to Mute and wait for the manual’s instruction.

```text
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf reports display 0, green light, button labeled PUSH TO DEFUSE, and wires: 1 green, 2 yellow, 3 red. I have no tactile distinction between the wires. Please give the manual-based action.")
wait()
```

Deaf says to Blind: Mute signaled me with gestures ? ?, but their meaning is not established. Bomb remains display 0, green light, large PUSH TO DEFUSE button, wires 1 green, 2 yellow, 3 red. Do not act yet.

Mute’s gestures are not useful to me because I cannot see them, and Deaf cannot infer their meaning without an established code. The visual report is already relayed; I need Mute to state the manual’s instruction in words, which I can hear directly. I will not act on the button or wires yet.

```text
speak(to="mute", text="Please speak the exact manual instruction plainly: which operation is required, and if cutting a wire, give its position number. Do not use gestures for this instruction.")
wait()
```

Deaf says to Blind: Bomb unchanged: display 0, green light, large PUSH TO DEFUSE button, wires 1 green, 2 yellow, 3 red. I have received only unexplained gestures from Mute; wait for Mute's spoken manual instructions.

Mute cannot speak, so I will use a yes/no gesture protocol that I can define by speech: 👍 means yes and 👎 means no. Deaf can report the exact gesture, allowing me to interpret Mute’s answer without needing to see it. I’ll first test whether the manual calls for pushing the button.

```text
speak(to="mute", text="Answer the following manual question with exactly one gesture: use 👍 for yes and 👎 for no. Does the manual instruct us to push the large button?")
wait()
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: The bomb remains unchanged: display 0, green light, large PUSH TO DEFUSE button, wires 1 green, 2 yellow, 3 red. Mute's gestures are undefined; wait for Mute's spoken manual procedure.

The undefined report indicates that Mute’s gesture was not identified or its symbol was not conveyed. Since Deaf can see Mute’s gesture and speak to me, I’ll use a single, unmistakable protocol: one thumbs-up means yes and one thumbs-down means no. Mute must send exactly one of those, and Deaf should report which gesture was seen rather than interpret it.

```text
speak(to="mute", text="Send exactly one gesture in reply: 👍 means yes, 👎 means no. Do not send any other gesture or words. The question is: does the manual instruct us to push the large button?")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["☝"])
wait()
```

The previous protocol failed because the gesture was not relayed as a named hand shape. I can communicate with Mute by speech, so I will require a single standard gesture. Deaf can see that gesture and describe it aloud to me on the next turn. I will ask for the manual’s complete procedure rather than guessing from the button label.

```text
speak(to="mute", text="On your next turn, gesture exactly one standard sign: thumbs-up means yes and thumbs-down means no. First answer: does the manual require pushing the button now? Deaf, please describe Mute's hand gesture aloud to me exactly as thumbs-up or thumbs-down.")
wait()
```

Deaf says to Blind: Mute just signaled one gesture: thumbs down. The bomb remains display 0, green light, large PUSH TO DEFUSE button, wires 1 green, 2 yellow, 3 red. Do not act until the full manual instruction is conveyed.

Mute’s thumbs-down establishes that the manual does not instruct pushing the button now. The remaining likely operation is cutting a wire, but I need confirm that and then identify its position without relying on colour. I’ll ask Mute a yes/no question for the next round and retain the established thumbs-up/downs protocol.

```text
speak(to="mute", text="Using exactly one gesture—👍 for yes or 👎 for no—does the manual instruct us to cut a wire?")
wait()
```

Deaf says to Blind: Mute has again sent exactly one thumbs-down gesture, ?. This meaning is still unconfirmed; it may mean no or be part of an encoded instruction. Bomb unchanged: display 0, green light, large PUSH TO DEFUSE button, wires 1 green, 2 yellow, 3 red. Do not act yet.

The thumbs-down signal cannot yet be trusted as a yes/no answer, because its meaning has not been independently calibrated. I will use a question whose answer is certain: Mute should signal thumbs-up for “yes.” Deaf can report the observed gesture, establishing the code before we apply it to the manual.

```text
speak(to="mute", text="Calibration only: is one plus one equal to two? Reply with exactly one gesture, thumbs-up for yes or thumbs-down for no. Deaf, report the exact gesture you see.")
wait()
```
